Attention: Angela Mahoney, General Manager
Dear Ms. Mahoney:

We are grateful for the confidence Lopez, Mcbride and Evans has placed in us, and we are writing to put down in one place, and in plain terms, the understanding on which we will carry out the ambulatory network study we have discussed with you and your colleagues over the last several weeks. Our aim is not to paper the relationship but to make certain that what we believe we have been asked to do, and the terms on which we have agreed to do it, are the same as what you understand them to be, so that we begin the work already agreed on its shape. If any part of this letter does not match your understanding, we would be glad to hear about it before you sign, and we will gladly revise it.
Scope of Our Work

You have asked us to assess the economic performance of the ambulatory surgery network that Lopez, Mcbride and Evans operates, and to help you see which of its service lines are carrying their share and which are not, so that the choices you make about capacity, staffing, and case mix rest on figures you are able to defend. We will assemble and reconcile the volume, charge, cost, and payer data that your finance and operations teams maintain; we will build a service-line view of contribution that ties back to your general ledger rather than floating free of it; and we will set our conclusions out in a written report in which the recommendations that follow are labeled plainly as recommendations, so that a reader can always see where the analysis ends and our judgment begins.

So that the edges of the work sit on the page rather than in anyone's memory, the study does not include a fair-market-value opinion on any physician arrangement, an audit of your financial statements, or advice on any particular transaction, and it does not reach any facility or entity beyond the ambulatory network we have named; each of those is work we are able to take up, and each would be the subject of its own letter. Our conclusions will describe the network as your data describes it to us, and should the underlying operations change in a way that bears on what we find, the analysis may no longer fit the network you are running, which is a limitation we want on the record from the start.
How We Will Approach It

We expect the work to move through three phases, and we describe them here so that you know what to expect of us and roughly when. In the first, we will gather and reconcile the source data alongside your teams and agree with them, in writing, on the definitions we are using, since a service-line study is only ever as trustworthy as the boundaries drawn around each line.

In the second, we will build the contribution analysis, reconcile it to your ledger, and test the assumptions that carry weight before we rely on any of them. In the third, we will write the report, review a draft of it with you so that any factual error about your operations is caught while it is still inexpensive to correct, and then deliver the final version with our recommendations kept distinct from our findings.
The People Who Will Do the Work

Daniel Alvarado, a Principal in our advisory practice, will lead the analysis and put his name to the report; service-line economics is the work he knows best, and he will be your point of contact on any question of method or finding. Barbara Freeman and Joshua Dougherty, analysts with us, will carry the data reconciliation and the contribution model, and you will see a good deal of them as they work with your finance and operations staff.

I will keep a partner's eye on the engagement throughout, and I will remain available to you on any matter of scope, staffing, or terms; if at any point the work or the people are not serving you as they should, I would ask only that you bring it to me early, while it is still easy to put right.
Fee and Timing

Our fee for the work described above is {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}, fixed for that scope, and we are prepared to begin on {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}. Any work you ask of us that falls outside the scope set out here will be quoted to you separately, and taken up only once we have told you in writing that it is additional and you have asked us, in writing, to proceed.
Fees and Payment

We will invoice against the fixed fee monthly as the work proceeds, and each invoice is due within thirty days of its date. Any out-of-pocket costs will be billed at cost and are not covered by the fee. We would always prefer to raise a question about an invoice with you directly and early, and we would ask the same courtesy of you.
Term and Termination

The engagement begins on the date named above and continues until we have delivered the final report and you have settled the fee for it. Either of us may bring it to an end on written notice, in which case you would owe us for the work properly done and the costs incurred to that point. We may also step back where our professional obligations require it, including were we ever asked to state a conclusion the analysis does not support, which is not a letter this firm will write.
Confidentiality

We will treat the information you share with us as confidential, use it only for this study, and hold our findings and our report in that same confidence. Because your data carries operational and financial detail you would not want circulated, we keep it within the team named above and dispose of it properly once the work is complete. We would ask, in turn, that you route any question about wider distribution of our report through us first, so that we can point out anything that ought to travel carefully.
Limitation of Liability

Our total liability arising out of this engagement is limited to the fees actually paid to us under it, and we are not responsible for indirect or consequential losses, lost profits among them. We say this not as a formality but because a service-line study is a considered judgment formed on the data available at a moment in time, and it cannot promise an outcome that turns on decisions and conditions lying outside our work. What you are engaging is our care and our judgment, exercised honestly and set out with their limits, and that is precisely what we undertake to give you.
Governing Law

This letter, and the work it describes, are governed by the law of the state in which our firm keeps its principal office, without regard to its conflict-of-laws rules. Should a disagreement over fees ever arise between us, we would each take part in that state bar's fee-dispute process before either of us carried the matter elsewhere.

If this letter sets out our understanding correctly, we would be grateful if you would sign the enclosed copy and return it to us, keeping the second for your own files; on receiving it, Daniel Alvarado will be in touch to arrange the opening session and the first request for data. We are glad to be taking up this work for Lopez, Mcbride and Evans, and we look forward to being of real and lasting use to you.
To: Daniel Alvarado, Principal; Joshua Dougherty, Analyst
From: Barbara Freeman, Analyst
Re: Kickoff, Ambulatory Network Study for Lopez, Mcbride and Evans

This memo sets out how we will run the ambulatory network study now that the engagement is confirmed. Our charge is a plain one. We are to tell {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} which of its service lines are earning their keep, and to do it with numbers that tie back to their ledger rather than float beside it.

The work begins on {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}, and I would like us aligned on its shape before then. The study is not technically hard. The difficulty lives in the definitions, and getting those right early is most of the work.

A word on tone, since we will be in front of their finance and operations people a good deal. We write for an audience that includes their general counsel, so we lead with the finding and let the recommendation follow, labeled as such. We do not assert a conclusion the analysis has not earned.

One note on the data itself. Their share is modern and mostly clean, so the pull should be straightforward, and I do not expect to spend long chasing files. The cost side is the exception, since service-line cost rarely lives in one report; we will build it from the general ledger and the case-costing detail together, and reconcile the two before we trust either.
I have set the lines of work out below, with where each of us starts. None of it is heavy yet, so this is the moment to raise anything that looks wrong to you.
Lines of Work

items: Data assembly. Owner: Barbara Freeman. I will pull the volume, charge, cost, and payer data from the client's finance and operations teams, by service line, and reconcile it to the general ledger before we build anything on top of it. Their ambulatory book runs across the usual outpatient lines, and I want each of them clean, not just the two or three that carry the volume. Nothing downstream is trustworthy until that reconciliation ties.

Service-line definitions. Owner: Joshua Dougherty. Agree the boundary of each service line with the client, in writing, including how shared and overhead costs are assigned. The contribution view is only as sound as these definitions, so we settle them before we count anything.

Contribution model. Owner: Barbara Freeman, with Daniel Alvarado reviewing the method. Build the service-line contribution analysis and tie it back to the ledger. Every sensitive assumption goes on the page where a reader can see it, not into a footnote.
Findings and client review. Owner: Daniel Alvarado. Draw the findings, keep every recommendation labeled as a recommendation, and review a draft with the client before anything is called final.

blocks.text: Where We Start

items: I will send the client our data request this week, so their finance team has the time to assemble it before we begin.
Joshua Dougherty to draft the service-line definitions for our internal review, before they go across to the client.
Daniel Alvarado to confirm the method for the contribution model, so we build it once and not twice.
We will hold a short standing check-in each week, so nothing waits a fortnight to surface.
Our client contact is Angela Mahoney, General Manager at Lopez, Mcbride and Evans. Please route client-facing questions through me, so she hears one voice from us.

blocks.text: That is the whole plan for now. The value this month is in the definitions, not the arithmetic. I will keep this memo current if anything shifts.
Minutes of our working session on the ambulatory network study for Lopez, Mcbride and Evans. Recorded by Daniel Alvarado.

blocks.text: Discussion

We are at the midpoint, and the picture is starting to resolve. The reconciled data holds, and the service-line contribution view now ties back to the ledger {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} maintains. That gives us a base we can trust, which is the thing we most needed before drawing any conclusion.

One note on the data before the substance. Their share is clean, so we spent no real time chasing files. The only rebuild was on the cost side, where we assembled service-line cost from the ledger and the case-costing detail and reconciled the two, and Barbara Freeman has that tie holding.

Barbara Freeman then walked the contribution model. Two service lines are clearly carrying the network, and their margins are not close calls. One line sits nearer the break-even point than the client had expected, and on first read the cause looks like payer mix rather than cost. We are treating that as a finding to confirm, not a conclusion to report.

The two strong lines are worth stating plainly even now. They are volume lines with a favorable payer mix, and nothing in the data threatens that read. We will still show the client the full contribution table rather than only the headline, because the value to them is in seeing the whole ranking.

Joshua Dougherty raised a fair question on the shared-cost allocation. It matters more than it sounds, because the marginal line moves across break-even depending on the method chosen. We agreed to run it both ways and show the client the sensitivity, instead of settling on one method quietly and presenting a single number.

Angela Mahoney asked whether we could name the weak line now. We said not yet, and we told her why. We have one open allocation question and one payer-mix effect still to confirm, and either could change the answer. She was comfortable waiting for the tested version, which is the right instinct.

On pace, we are where we planned to be at this stage. The work still ahead is confirmation more than discovery. We are keeping recommendations out of these minutes on purpose; they belong in the report, set after the findings that carry them.

We also settled the cadence. Barbara Freeman will refresh the reconciliation against the client's latest extract, and we will hold the next working session once the two open items are tested. Nothing agreed here is left to memory; the items below carry an owner against each.
Action Items

rows: Confirm the payer-mix effect on the marginal service line
Run the shared-cost allocation both ways and quantify the swing
Reconcile the latest data extract to the client's ledger
Send the client the questions on their case-mix coding
Circulate the full contribution table ahead of the next session

blocks.text: Status Report: Ambulatory Network Study for Lopez, Mcbride and Evans
Prepared for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}. Prepared by Barbara Freeman, Analyst, and reviewed by Daniel Alvarado, Principal, before it was sent.
Where the Work Stands

The study is at its midpoint and on plan. The reconciled data is holding, and the service-line contribution view now ties to your ledger. We have a base we trust, and the work ahead is confirmation more than construction.

The share your teams gave us was clean, which has kept us on schedule. The only real build was on the cost side, which we assembled from the general ledger and the case-costing detail and reconciled, rather than taking either as given.

The engagement is running against its fixed budget of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}, and the effort spent to date is roughly half of that, which is where it should sit at the halfway mark. Nothing in this report is a final finding. We mark clearly what is settled and what we are still testing.
This Period
The work this period was mostly assembly and first analysis. We completed the following.

items: Assembled and reconciled the volume, charge, cost, and payer data with your finance team, by service line, and tied it back to the general ledger, so that every figure we report can be traced to a source.
Agreed the service-line definitions with your operations team, including how shared and overhead costs are assigned, and recorded them in writing so the boundaries are not in dispute later.
Built the service-line contribution model on those definitions, with the sensitive assumptions recorded on the page rather than buried in the workbook.
Identified the two service lines carrying the network and one line sitting close to break-even, which we are still testing before we are willing to call it.
Reviewed the method with Daniel Alvarado and set the questions we need answered on case-mix coding.

blocks.text: Coming Up
The next period turns from building the model to confirming what it shows. We plan to do the following.

items: Confirm whether the marginal service line's position is driven by payer mix or by cost. Joshua Dougherty is running that analysis now.
Run the shared-cost allocation two ways and show you the sensitivity, so you can see how much the answer depends on the method.
Draft the findings, with recommendations set apart and labeled as recommendations.
Review a draft of the report with you before it is final, so that any factual error about your operations is corrected while it is still cheap to fix.

blocks.text: What We Need From You
Two things from your team would keep us on the current pace, and neither is urgent this week. We set them out now so there is time to gather them.

items: The case-mix coding detail behind the outpatient volumes, so we can confirm that the service each line records is the service it delivered.
A short session with whoever owns the cost allocation, so our method matches how you actually run the accounting rather than how we assume you do.

blocks.text: Risks and Watch Items
Three items could still move the findings, and we want them on your radar.

items: Case-mix coding. If the coding we are given does not match the service the network actually delivered, the contribution by line will shift. We have asked your team for the coding detail and will flag any gap we find.
Allocation method. One service line crosses break-even depending on how shared cost is assigned. We will show you the swing plainly, not fold it into a single number.
Data completeness. Our conclusions describe the network as your data describes it to us. A material gap in the source data is a limit on the finding, and we will say so plainly.

blocks.text: Budget

We remain on plan and within the fixed budget of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}. No part of the work to date has fallen outside the scope set in the engagement letter, and we would tell you in writing before taking up anything that did.

The next report will carry the tested findings on the marginal service line. If anything in your operations changed during this period that we ought to factor in, please tell us before we draft, while it is still easy to fold in.
Minutes of our working session on the ambulatory network study for Lopez, Mcbride and Evans. Recorded by Daniel Alvarado.

blocks.text: Discussion

We are near the end, and the findings hold. The marginal service line came down to payer mix, not cost, and we can now say so with the data standing behind it. That was the last open question of any substance.

Barbara Freeman closed the reconciliation. The contribution view ties to the ledger {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} maintains at every line, and nothing in the final extract moved a service line across the break-even boundary. The base is settled.

The picture is a clean one. The two strong lines carry the network on volume and a favorable payer mix. The rest sit above their cost, save the one weak line, which does not cover its cost, and the reason is the payer mix it draws rather than how it is run.

Joshua Dougherty finished the allocation sensitivity. Both methods leave the two strong lines strong and the weak line weak, so the conclusion does not depend on the choice. The client asked for that comparison specifically, and it is reassuring to be able to give the same answer either way.

Angela Mahoney asked whether the weak line should be read as a recommendation to close it. We said no, and we were careful about the distinction. Our finding is that the line does not cover its cost at the current payer mix. What the client decides to do about that is a decision for the client, and the report will label our recommendation as a recommendation, kept separate from the finding.

We also talked through the options the report will lay out, without ranking them here. A shift in payer mix, a change in the case scheduled to that line, and consolidation onto fewer sessions each change the arithmetic in a different way. We will show the effect of each and let the client weigh them.

We agreed the shape of the report. Findings first, recommendations after and labeled as such, and the allocation sensitivity documented in an appendix, so the client can see the working. Barbara Freeman and Joshua Dougherty will square away the tables while the drafting is under way.
On pace, we are in the last stretch. What remains is drafting and review, not analysis. We will bring a draft to the client for a factual read before anything is called final.
Action Items

rows: Draft the findings section, with recommendations set apart and labeled
Finalize the contribution tables and assumption log
Document the allocation sensitivity for the appendix
Lay out the options on the weak service line, without ranking them
Schedule the draft review with the client
